correctness.rationale: The derived line Kz is invariant under derivations. For B=diag(1,d), Leibniz on V×V is MᵀB+BM=cB. With char K≠2 and d≠0 this gives exactly M=aI+bJ_d and c=2a; the V→Kz functional is free. For a single nonzero projected input v, any chosen a,b matching Nv can be completed by a functional with the prescribed central value, and on tz one uses a=c/2. Thus locality is equivalent to Nv∈span(v,J_d v) plus preservation of Kz. The evaluation determinant is x²+dy². This gives no restriction on N in the anisotropic case and preservation of the two distinct J_d eigenlines in the split case, yielding the claimed dimensions 7 and 5. For linear 2-local maps the pair (e1,e2) fixes the projected block aI+bJ_d, and the pair (e1,e1+z) forces c=2a because evaluation at e1 is injective on that block. The homogeneous nonadditive central-valued example interpolates on every pair by one linear functional. The base-change witness N=diag(1,0) takes (±√(−d),1) off its isotropic line in the separable quadratic extension. A fresh exhaustive F3 test derives the 81 derivations from the Leibniz rule over all 3×3 linear maps and checks actual single- and pair-evaluation membership: 2187 or 243 local maps, and exactly the 81 derivations in both linear 2-local cases.
residual_risks: The replay is over F3 only. The proof does not require field infinitude or characteristic zero, but it excludes char 2 and d=0 throughout. It neither classifies nor counts nonlinear 2-local maps.

value.rationale: A split/anisotropic distinction on a standard minimal nondegenerate multiplication form gives an explicit two-dimensional jump in the space of local maps, although the derivation space does not change. The separable base-change witness explains why an algebraically closed classification alone loses arithmetic information. The fact that linear 2-locality is rigid on both sides of the same jump makes this a useful boundary example rather than a bare finite-field count.
residual_risks: The example does not establish higher-dimensional form classifications or a general base-change theorem.
